name: Lime
summary: Limes are small, sharp green citrus fruit used for their juice and zest in food and drinks. This page lists what people say limes do; each claim can be checked against the research when you choose.
inIt: Lime (Citrus aurantiifolia) is used fresh, in food, sweets and drinks, and its oils in cosmetics and medicines, according to a 2021 review. The molecules behind its phototoxic skin reactions belong to the coumarin and furocoumarin families.

The UK food table (CoFID) measures fresh lime juice at 9 kcal, 1.6 g of sugars, 110 mg of potassium, 9 mg of calcium and 38 mg of vitamin C per 100 g. Lime flesh has 46 mg of vitamin C per 100 g. The table does not measure the coumarins or the other plant compounds.
Lime and lemon are different fruit, and their juices read alike in the table: 38 mg of vitamin C per 100 g in fresh lime juice, 36 mg in fresh lemon juice.
processing: Cordial is not juice: the UK food table lists undiluted lime juice cordial at 29.8 g of sugars and no vitamin C per 100 g, against 1.6 g of sugars and 38 mg of vitamin C in fresh lime juice.
Citrus fruit and juice taken often can wear teeth: a 2014 review names the fruit's acidity, how it is taken and how long teeth are exposed.

whoShouldBeCareful.with: Lime juice or peel on skin in sunlight
whoShouldBeCareful.note: A 2026 review describes margarita dermatitis: lime juice or peel on the skin followed by sun exposure causes painful redness and blisters, often followed by dark marks that fade. Many people do not link it to the lime. If you get a rash or blisters after handling limes in the sun, talk to your doctor.

A 2021 review says the main adverse reactions to lime are allergic or phototoxic contact dermatitis, and that reactions to eating the fruit seem rare, with no known cases in the literature. If you react to limes or citrus oils, talk to your doctor or an allergist.
